name: Explore
purpose: Collect possibilities before choosing a direction.

state.title: Explore · fictional example
state.question: What could our bookshop do with its spare room?
state.context: Fictional bookshop: a spare room is available; demand, costs and the preferred use are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: Which possibility is worth developing, or what else could we add?

nodes.label: What could the spare room become?
nodes.notes: Open ideation about uses of the room. The suggestions are neither exhaustive nor ranked; no option has been investigated.
nodes.source:
Method background: McKinsey: seven-step problem solving
https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/our-insights/how-to-master-the-seven-step-problem-solving-process
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Paid workshops
nodes.notes: A possible use, with pricing and demand still unknown.

nodes.label: Beginner writing sessions
nodes.notes: One possible workshop format. Instructor availability, willingness to pay and resource needs remain unknown.

nodes.label: A quiet reading room
nodes.notes: Another possible use. Reader interest, access arrangements and operating costs remain open.

nodes.label: Keep it as storage
nodes.notes: Retain the current assumed use. Establish its operational value before treating it as wasted space.

uncertainties: Preferred outcome, demand, resources and costs.

name: Issue tree
purpose: Break a question into answerable parts.

state.title: Issue tree · fictional example
state.question: Could paid workshops be viable next quarter?
state.context: Fictional bookshop: tickets might cost £20 and five staff-hours are available weekly; demand, delivery needs and complete costs are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: Which answer would most change the workshop decision?

nodes.label: Could paid workshops be viable?
nodes.notes: An initial viability inquiry for next quarter: demand at a viable price, delivery within constraints and economics. These questions interact and do not constitute exhaustive market-entry due diligence.
nodes.source:
Method background: McKinsey: seven-step problem solving
https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/our-insights/how-to-master-the-seven-step-problem-solving-process
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Would enough people pay?
nodes.notes: Investigate paying demand for a particular subject and date at the proposed price.

nodes.label: How many would book at £20?
nodes.notes: Unknown. Check paid booking evidence and cancellation terms; stated interest is not a purchase commitment.

nodes.label: Can we deliver it?
nodes.notes: Investigate staff time, room capacity and dependencies before assuming that an event can run as costed.

nodes.label: Will it fit five staff-hours?
nodes.notes: Five available staff-hours a week is a fictional constraint. Preparation, hosting and follow-up time still need estimating.

nodes.label: Would it cover relevant costs?
nodes.notes: Investigate contribution and fixed costs using a consistent event and time basis.

nodes.label: What attendance breaks even?
nodes.notes: Unknown until the relevant fixed costs, ticket price and variable costs are established. This hurdle alone cannot prove demand.

name: Hypothesis tree
purpose: Test an explanation, including what could disprove it.

state.title: Hypothesis tree · fictional example
state.question: Did a later workshop start time reduce attendance?
state.context: Fictional bookshop: attendance fell after a schedule change, but the cause and comparison evidence are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: What evidence would separate a timing problem from weaker topic appeal?

nodes.label: Later start reduced attendance?
nodes.notes: A provisional causal explanation. Topic appeal and promotion are plausible competing explanations; several causes may coexist. The checks below are diagnostic, not collectively sufficient proof of causation.
nodes.source:
Method background: Victor Cheng: issue trees
https://caseinterview.com/issue-tree
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Did the decline follow the change?
nodes.notes: Compare the dated schedule change with attendance over time. A decline starting earlier would challenge this explanation; a later decline alone would not prove it.

nodes.label: Do customers report time clashes?
nodes.notes: Look for relevant customer evidence, which has not been supplied. Reports may support the proposed mechanism but can be selective or retrospective.

nodes.label: Did old-time sessions hold up?
nodes.notes: Compare sessions at the old time while checking topic, audience, price and promotion differences. No comparison result is assumed.

nodes.label: Could the topics be less appealing?
nodes.notes: A competing explanation to investigate. Compare like-for-like topics and promotion before attributing changes to the start time.

name: Driver tree
purpose: Show the arithmetic behind a number.

state.title: Driver tree · fictional example
state.question: How many paying attendees would cover one workshop’s costs?
state.context: Fictional workshop: £120 fixed cost, £20 tickets and £5 variable cost per attendee are teaching inputs; demand and capacity remain unknown.
state.nextQuestion: What happens to break-even if the variable cost rises?

nodes.label: Break-even: £120 ÷ £15 = 8 people
nodes.notes: For one event, minimum paying attendance = ceil(fixed cost / (ticket price − variable cost per attendee)). The contribution must be positive. Round fractional attendance up. Costs and prices are assumed constant across the relevant range; this is a hurdle, not a demand forecast.
nodes.source:
Method background: McKinsey: Electro-Light teaching case
https://www.mckinsey.com/careers/interviewing/electrolight
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Fixed cost: £120 per event
nodes.notes: Stipulated input for one workshop. Real use requires checking complete relevant fixed costs and any capacity thresholds.

nodes.label: Contribution: £20 − £5 = £15
nodes.notes: Contribution per attendee = ticket price per attendee − variable cost per attendee. Under these fictional inputs, £15 per attendee remains towards fixed costs.

nodes.label: Ticket price: £20 per person
nodes.notes: Stipulated price; no evidence that customers will pay it has been supplied.

nodes.label: Variable cost: £5 per person
nodes.notes: Stipulated total variable cost per attendee. Verify materials, payment charges and other attendance-dependent costs in a real case.

decision.rationale: Eight paying attendees cover the stated costs; demand, capacity and cost completeness remain open.

name: Solution tree
purpose: Connect an improvement to levers and possible actions.

state.title: Solution tree · fictional example
state.question: How could the bookshop reduce Saturday queues below five minutes?
state.context: Fictional bookshop: queues are the problem; the bottleneck, customer response and staffing options are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: Which part of the queue is actually limiting service?

nodes.label: Reduce Saturday queue time
nodes.notes: Desired improvement during Saturday peaks. The three levers are proposed mechanisms that can combine, not proven causes or mutually exclusive options. This is a practical how-tree example, not a named Bain taxonomy.
nodes.source:
Method background: Bain: FashionCo. teaching case
https://www.bain.com/careers/hiring-process/interviewing/fashion-case-study/
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Fewer arrivals at peak time
nodes.notes: Moving some arrivals to quieter periods could reduce peak demand. This depends on customers being able and willing to change time.

nodes.label: Offer quieter collection windows
nodes.notes: A proposed intervention to shift collection traffic. Assess existing arrival patterns and customer flexibility before choosing it.

nodes.label: More peak service capacity
nodes.notes: Extra effective service capacity could reduce waiting. A shared packing or payment bottleneck might prevent the gain.

nodes.label: Staff a second till
nodes.notes: A proposed intervention. Confirm staff availability, cost and whether both tills can process orders independently.

nodes.label: Shorter transactions
nodes.notes: Less work at the counter could increase throughput, provided the work is removed or completed beforehand.

nodes.label: Prepare collection orders early
nodes.notes: A proposed intervention to reduce counter work. Check whether preparation can be moved outside the peak without causing other delays.

name: Objectives tree
purpose: Clarify what a good choice should provide.

state.title: Objectives tree · fictional example
state.question: What would make a job offer suitable?
state.context: Fictional job seeker: financial security, autonomy and learning are stated priorities; offers, trade-offs and personal weights are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: What would good performance on each objective look like?

nodes.label: What makes a suitable job?
nodes.notes: A hierarchy of desired ends for this fictional person, not a universal list of job criteria. Actual offers should be assessed against clear descriptions; no weights are invented.
nodes.source:
Method background: Keeney and colleagues: value-focused planning
https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/780189
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Financial security
nodes.notes: The desired end is reliable capacity to meet commitments, rather than simply choosing the highest headline salary.

nodes.label: Reliable income covers commitments
nodes.notes: Use the person’s actual commitments and a consistent after-tax income period when assessing offers. No amount has been supplied.

nodes.label: Autonomy
nodes.notes: The desired end is control over how work is carried out. Remote work could be a means, but does not automatically provide autonomy.

nodes.label: Control over how work is done
nodes.notes: Describe which decisions the person wants to control, then inspect what each role permits.

nodes.label: Learning
nodes.notes: The desired end is developing chosen capabilities; a course budget alone does not establish that learning occurs.

nodes.label: Regular practice and useful feedback
nodes.notes: Look for opportunities to practise the chosen skills and receive feedback in the role. Skill priorities and offer evidence are unknown.

name: Decision tree
purpose: Compare choices when outcomes are uncertain.

source.title: Open University: decision trees and expected value

state.title: Decision tree · fictional example
state.question: Should we hold or cancel one event?
state.context: Fictional event: probabilities and net payoffs are stipulated for teaching; risk tolerance and non-financial effects are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: Would the possible £100 loss change the choice for this person?

nodes.label: Hold or cancel the event?
nodes.notes: Choose before attendance is known. Under the stipulated two-outcome model, holding has expected net payoff 0.6 × £200 + 0.4 × (−£100) = £80, versus £0 for cancelling. Expected value alone does not settle risk tolerance or non-financial objectives.
nodes.source:
Method background: Open University: decision trees and expected value
https://www.open.edu/openlearn/money-business/decision-trees-and-dealing-uncertainty/content-section-4.1
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Hold the event
nodes.notes: A controllable choice taken before observing attendance. All event costs are already included in the terminal net payoffs; do not subtract them again.

nodes.label: Attendance is uncertain
nodes.notes: Conditional on holding, strong and weak attendance are stipulated to be the only possible outcomes, mutually exclusive and exhaustive, with probabilities 0.6 and 0.4. These are illustrative assumptions, not estimated demand.

nodes.label: Strong: 60% → +£200 net
nodes.notes: Conditional probability P(strong attendance | hold) = 0.6. Net payoff for this one event is +£200 after all relevant event costs.

nodes.label: Weak: 40% → −£100 net
nodes.notes: Conditional probability P(weak attendance | hold) = 0.4. Net payoff for this one event is −£100 after all relevant event costs.

nodes.label: Cancel the event
nodes.notes: The alternative controllable choice in this simplified model; cancellation has no remaining fees or other monetary effects by stipulation.

nodes.label: Net payoff: £0
nodes.notes: Certain net payoff under the fictional cancellation assumption, on the same one-event basis as the holding payoffs.

decision.rationale: Expected monetary value is £80 for holding and £0 for cancelling under the stated assumptions; the broader choice remains open.

name: Opportunity tree
purpose: Connect customer needs to solutions and assumption tests.

state.title: Opportunity tree · fictional example
state.question: How could a booking product increase completed bookings?
state.context: Fictional booking product: difficulty finding a suitable time is a proposed customer need awaiting research; solution effects are unknown.
state.nextQuestion: What customer research supports the need before we develop a solution?

nodes.label: Increase completed bookings
nodes.notes: The desired product outcome. Specify a consistent measurement period and eligible customer population in real use. This example shows one proposed opportunity, not a researched or complete opportunity space.
nodes.source:
Method background: Teresa Torres: opportunity solution trees
https://www.producttalk.org/opportunity-solution-trees/
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Find a time that fits
nodes.notes: A proposed customer opportunity, not an observed need. Research must establish whether this difficulty exists, for whom, and whether addressing it could increase completed bookings.

nodes.label: Flexible-date search
nodes.notes: One possible response to difficulty finding a suitable time. It assumes customers can be flexible and that acceptable alternatives exist.

nodes.label: Can users find an acceptable slot?
nodes.notes: A proposed task-based prototype check of whether flexible dates reveal a time the customer can actually use. It does not by itself prove a rise in completed bookings.

nodes.label: Availability alerts
nodes.notes: Another possible response. It assumes a suitable opening occurs and reaches the customer while booking intent remains.

nodes.label: Does the alert arrive in time?
nodes.notes: Check the assumption that openings and alerts occur before customers give up or book elsewhere. No test has run and no customer behaviour is claimed.

name: Argument tree
purpose: Show a conclusion, its reasons and the counterargument.

state.title: Argument tree · fictional example
state.question: Why try one workshop before committing to a recurring programme?
state.context: Fictional bookshop: interest is non-binding and one event has no ongoing contract by stipulation; repeat demand and pilot transfer remain unknown.
state.nextQuestion: Would one event tell us enough about a recurring programme?

nodes.label: Try one workshop first (provisional)
nodes.notes: A bounded provisional conclusion from the fictional premises below, using the argument-hierarchy component of Minto’s Pyramid Principle. It assumes the one-event cost is acceptable and the pilot can inform the next decision; no actual results are supplied.
nodes.source:
Method background: Barbara Minto: the Pyramid Principle
https://www.mckinsey.com/alumni/news-and-events/global-news/alumni-news/barbara-minto-mece-i-invented-it-so-i-get-to-say-how-to-pronounce-it
The case and its inputs are fictional teaching material from Strategy Canvas, not findings from this source.

nodes.label: Recurring demand is unproven
nodes.notes: Non-binding interest leaves payment and repeat attendance uncertain, so it is a weak basis for a recurring commitment.

nodes.label: Interest is non-binding (assumed)
nodes.notes: Explicit fictional stipulation, not observed customer evidence: the available expressions of interest involve no purchase commitment.

nodes.label: A pilot can test paid uptake
nodes.notes: A paid offer could reveal uptake under that offer’s conditions. The inference depends on the audience, price and format being informative for the planned programme.

nodes.label: One event limits commitment
nodes.notes: A single event avoids committing to future sessions under the fictional contract premise; the initial event still has a cost.

nodes.label: No ongoing contract (assumed)
nodes.notes: Explicit fictional stipulation: venue and staffing commitments end after this event. In a real case, inspect the actual terms before relying on this premise.

nodes.label: One event may not predict repeats
nodes.notes: Material counterargument: novelty, a special audience or a one-off topic could make pilot uptake a poor guide to recurring demand. This limits how far the conclusion can extend.

decision.rationale: A small commitment may test paid uptake while demand is unproven, provided its cost is acceptable and its conditions inform the next decision.
uncertainties: Whether one event can inform recurring demand.
Whether the initial event cost is acceptable.
